                 ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA
                TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION’S RESPONSE TO
            4K LAND AND CATTLE COMPANY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 13

        4K Land and Cattle Company has appealed SOAH Order No. 13, which denied the requests

for a route adequacy hearing and canceled the hearing scheduled for May 18, 2026. 1 In its Appeal,

4K Land and Cattle Company recycles the same arguments the ALJs already considered and

rejected—contending that the study area should be expanded north and comparing it to Oncor’s

Dinosaur Switch to Longshore Switch 765 kV transmission line project (“Dinosaur to Longshore”). 2

Notably, 4K Land and Cattle Company did not attempt to make any showing that the number and

combination possibilities of routing options in the Application are too few in number, or even attempt

to propose any superior alternative routes for the Commission’s consideration; rather, it offered only


        1
          4K Land and Cattle Company’s Appeal of SOAH Order No. 13 Denying Motions for Route Adequacy Hearing
at 1 (May 26, 2026) (Item No. 5151) (Appeal).
        2
            Id. at 2.


ONCOR AND LCRA TSC’S RESPONSE TO 4K LAND AND CATTLE COMPANY’S
APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 13

                                                 Page 1 of 8
 amorphous commentary suggesting that the study area should have been expanded. 3 For the reasons

set forth below, the appeal lacks merit.

                                           I.     ANALYSIS

   A. The Application presents an adequate number of reasonably differentiated alternatives
      supported by a reasoned justification.

       The Application includes 122 geographically diverse routes comprised of 171 alternative

route links, offering thousands of potential forward-progressing routes to connect the Project’s

endpoints across a geographic area spanning approximately 200 miles east-to-west and 35 miles

north-to-south. 4 The ALJs found this showing sufficient, concluding that “the Application provides

an adequate number of reasonably differentiated alternative routes to conduct a proper evaluation”

and that “Applicants have established the specific geographic and regulatory constraints that shaped

such corridors.” 5

       In its Appeal and its initial route adequacy challenge, 4K Land and Cattle Company did not

challenge the number of routing options, propose any allegedly superior route, or identify any specific

routing alternative that should have been included. Instead, it offers only generalized commentary

that routes should have been studied to the north. 6 But such arguments do not overcome the fact that

Fort Hood and dense commercial and residential areas surrounding it, including Temple, Belton,

Killeen, Harker Heights, and Copperas Cove, significantly constrain northern expansion. 7

APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 13

         As explained in the Applicants’ Consolidated Response—and reiterated by the ALJs in SOAH

Order No. 13—Bell County East Switch and Big Hill Substation sit at approximately the same

latitude. 8 Therefore, routes that swing far north or south “would necessarily double-back, increasing

mileage and costs, and running contrary to the requirement that routing alternatives be reasonably

forward progressing.” 9

        4K Land and Cattle Company continues to compare the Project’s study area to Dinosaur to

Longshore, relying upon its so-called “centerline gravity index,” a metric that, to Applicants’

knowledge, has never been cited or relied upon in any CCN proceeding before the Commission. 10 As

Applicants have explained, the two study areas are in different parts of the state and have their own

unique set of constraints that influence study area size and shape. 11 These study areas cannot be

considered in a vacuum, as 4K Land and Cattle Company seeks to do. 12 If the Commission were to

require every study area to be larger than the one that came before it, study areas for all projects would

continue to expand arbitrarily, impacting more and more landowners unnecessarily. 13

        4K Land and Cattle Company also erroneously analogizes this Project to Docket Nos. 32070

and 41606. 14 This Project is distinguishable from both.

           Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation’s Consolidated
Response to Route Adequacy Challenges at 13 (May 13, 2026) (Item No. 4515) (Applicants’ Consolidated Response);
SOAH Order No. 13 at 7.

         Docket No. 32070 involved a proposed substation, a facility that the applicant itself selected

and sited, and the Commission determined that the location of that proposed substation should not

constrain the analysis of adequate alternative routes. 15 That concern is absent here. Unlike Docket

No. 32070, ERCOT identified the Project’s endpoints, Bell County East Switch and Big Hill

Substation, in connection with the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. These endpoints exist today and

will be expanded to accommodate the 765 kV transmission line. Moreover, 4K Land and Cattle

Company does not contest the selected endpoints but instead objects to the lack of northern routes. 16

This is not a self-imposed limitation. Rather, it is an unavoidable geographic constraint arising from

Fort Hood’s fixed footprint, which precludes routing to the north without significant doubling-back. 17

        In Docket No. 41606, the ALJ rejected constraining all proposed routes through a routing

circle of approximately three miles in diameter and required additional route combinations using

previously noticed links that did not pass through the circle. 18 Applicants distinguished that case in

their Consolidated Response, and the ALJs agreed that the constraints Applicants identified, including

Fort Hood and Lake Buchanan, were appropriate. 19

          Application of Wood County Electric Cooperative, Inc. for a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for a
Proposed Transmission Line in Wood County Texas, Docket No. 32070, Order on Appeal of Order No. 8 at 6 (Nov. 1,
2006).

Line in Hidalgo and Cameron Counties, Docket No. 41606, SOAH Order No. 6 (Oct. 21, 2013).

established the specific geographic and regulatory constraints that shaped such corridors).


ONCOR AND LCRA TSC’S RESPONSE TO 4K LAND AND CATTLE COMPANY’S
APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 13

                                                    Page 4 of 8
    B. 4K Land and Cattle Company’s criticism of Applicants’ methodology is not a proper
      adequacy challenge.

       4K Land and Cattle Company contends that SOAH Order No. 13 ignores their claim that

Applicants’ alleged lack of methodology produced a narrow study area. 20 The ALJs, however, found

the study area reasonable and the routes are adequately diverse, rejecting that contention. 21 Moreover,

a route adequacy challenge does not turn on the methodology used to prepare the Environmental

Assessment. The relevant question is whether the Application presents an adequate number of

alternative routes to allow meaningful evaluation, and the ALJs have already determined that it

does. 22 That determination does not require a dissection of the methodology used to identify the site

and the routes.

       Nonetheless, Applicants and other utilities have successfully utilized the same, or

substantially the same, practice to prepare an Environmental Assessment within the ERCOT market

for decades. 23     Neither the Public Utility Regulatory Act, nor the Commission Rules require

Applicants to apply the Electric Power Research Institute – Georgia Transmission Committee (EPRI–

GTC) methodology in conducting an Environmental Assessment. And Applicants have not located

a single instance where EPRI–GTC methodology was referenced or relied upon in an ERCOT CCN

proceeding. Additionally, 4K Land and Cattle Company’s claim that Applicants disregarded Texas

ONCOR AND LCRA TSC’S RESPONSE TO 4K LAND AND CATTLE COMPANY’S
APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 13

                                               Page 5 of 8
 Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) resources is unfounded. Applicants coordinated extensively

with the TPWD. 24 Even so, TPWD comments are not binding on utilities or the Commission. 25

    C. The Project’s voltage does not require expansion of the study area.

        4K Land and Cattle Company argues that the higher voltage of the Project demands broader

alternatives. 26 It does not. Applicants are not aware of a statute, rule, or precedent that supports

expanding a study area based solely on a project’s first-time nature. On the contrary, such a

requirement would arbitrarily expand study areas over time. 27

        4K Land and Cattle Company argues that Project cost alone warrants further examination and

cites Docket No. 38354 as precedent for the Commission approving a more costly route where the

less costly option does not outweigh the benefits of parallel ROW. 28 However, cost of a project alone

does not justify a route adequacy challenge, and route adequacy in this Project does not depend solely

on the length of parallel ROW. Applicants evaluated all required statutory criteria and proposed a

diverse set of routes, which the ALJs have already found sufficient. 29

                                              II.       CONCLUSION

        Applicants respectfully request that the Commission deny 4K Land and Cattle Company’s

Appeal of SOAH Order No. 13. The ALJs have considered arguments and the Applicants’ reasoned

 justification for the alternative routes presented and subsequently reached a well-supported

conclusion that the Application provides an adequate number of reasonably differentiated alternative

routes. 4K Land and Cattle Company did not make a showing of route inadequacy or propose any

superior alternative routes; rather, it offered only vague commentary regarding expansion northward.

Dissatisfaction with the size of the study area does not establish that the ALJs erred. No route

adequacy hearing is warranted.
